weekly_note.text: This week: inflation reasserted itself on both the consumer and producer sides, consumer sentiment cratered, and the cost of building with AI kept falling. The economy split into two stories at once.

weekly_connection.title: The squeezed customer, the cheaper build
weekly_connection.subtitle: Inflation pressure and weak sentiment are climbing while the cost of building with AI keeps falling — the economy split into two stories at once.
body_paragraphs: These three numbers usually don't all move in the same week. Consumer prices reaccelerated. Consumer sentiment dropped to readings rarely seen. And AI model costs continued to fall fast. Two of those make customers tougher to win; one makes it cheaper than ever to ship the thing that could earn them.

What I keep coming back to: the customer side and the build side are pulling in opposite directions. The product moves that work right now are the ones that build on the deflationary side of the split — leveraging cheap AI to do more for a stressed buyer — rather than the ones that count on the buyer feeling flush.

refined.observation: Headline inflation heated back up rather than cooling — with energy doing most of the lifting. Consumer sentiment is sitting near record-low readings and households expect prices to keep rising. Meanwhile, AI model costs keep falling sharply across major labs.
refined.why_it_matters: Your customer is feeling worse and paying more for the things they can't avoid. Your cost of shipping AI capability into your product has rarely been lower. Plans calibrated for a calmer, more confident consumer need a second look — and plans that lean on AI leverage just got cheaper to test.
refined.decision_this_week: Which roadmap item still assumes a confident buyer with extra discretionary spend? Pick one and ask whether the cheaper-AI side of the split changes how you'd ship it.
refined.pm_implication_default: The PMs winning this environment make the cheap path through the product obvious, use cheaper AI to do more for a stressed buyer instead of charging them more, and stop assuming the customer feels the way they did six months ago.

where_shows_up.label: Onboarding
where_shows_up.implication: A stressed buyer with elevated inflation expectations has less patience for setup. Time-to-first-value matters more than the breadth of the tour.

where_shows_up.label: Pricing
where_shows_up.implication: Make the cheap path obvious. Cheaper AI calls let you include more in lower tiers without breaking the math — that lands better than a price hike right now.

where_shows_up.label: Support
where_shows_up.implication: Support is where AI leverage pays back fastest. Cheaper calls plus a stressed customer make "deflect with a useful answer" the easiest ROI to show.

where_shows_up.label: Workflows
where_shows_up.implication: Workflows that still hand work to the user are exposed. Cheaper inference means the model can quietly finish more steps without costing you the margin.

where_shows_up.label: Retention
where_shows_up.implication: Downgrade paths matter more than churn-prevention emails. Make the cheaper plan visible before the cancel button is.

weekly_thought.headline: The same year hiring got hardest in a decade, AI got the cheapest it's ever been to deploy.

build.label: Build Decisions
build.pattern: Most people aren't holding both of these in their head at once. [chip:tech-hiring] is at its lowest in a decade, while [chip:ai-api-pricing] just hit the cheapest it's ever been. Roadmap items you deferred for headcount last quarter might be shippable this quarter — for a completely different reason. For example: a support team that couldn't get two more engineers six months ago could now ship a deflection feature that the model finishes for them.
build.action: Which project on your deferred list assumes you need to hire to ship it?

customer.label: Customer Behavior
customer.pattern: Your buyers are quieter, not poorer. [chip:consumer-confidence] has cratered, but [chip:retail-sales] is still running near 5% year-over-year. Sentiment surveys are louder than wallets right now — and the gap between them is widening. For example: a SaaS team running a Pro tier upgrade campaign might find their conversion math is unchanged but their churn-risk profile quietly worse.
customer.action: When your users tell you they're tightening their belts, which number do you trust — what they say, or what they spend?

business.label: Business Reality
business.pattern: Budgets for next quarter are being written around two numbers moving in opposite directions. Teams plan headcount against [chip:tech-hiring] staying tight, then quietly fund tooling against [chip:compute-cost] falling. The line item that used to read 'hire two engineers' is becoming 'buy more inference.' For example: an early-stage team writing their Q3 plan might cap headcount one head lower and add a $2K/month tooling line — and still ship more.
business.action: Open next quarter's plan and find the one hire you'd swap for tooling if the model could do 70% of the job.

future.label: Future Signals
future.pattern: The thing to watch isn't the price drop itself — it's how fast new models keep landing. [chip:ai-model-releases] are shipping faster than they have since 2024, and each one resets what 'too expensive to automate' means. The deferred-work list isn't fixed; it shrinks every few weeks on its own. For example: a workflow you ruled out as 'too expensive to automate' six months ago might be cheap enough now that it's the obvious next feature.
future.action: Write down one task you ruled out as 'not worth automating' six months ago, and ask whether that's still true.

pm_tension.label: This week's PM tension
pm_tension.question: Does your plan still assume a buyer who feels better than the one you actually have?
pm_tension.note: A question worth holding open this week — not a recommendation.

toggles.question: What workflow still assumes more people instead of better leverage?
toggles.note: Build-vs-wait: with inference cheap and the customer stressed, the cost of waiting on a small AI feature that helps the buyer has shifted.

toggles.question: Which line on the deck has to improve before your next funding conversation — top of funnel, or unit economics?
toggles.note: Growth-vs-efficiency: capital is concentrating; the slide that wins the next round looks different than it did 24 months ago.

toggles.question: Where are you optimizing for being early — and where are you optimizing for being right?
toggles.note: Speed-vs-certainty: model capability moves fast enough that a six-month bet on a feasibility gap can close before launch.

toggles.question: Which step of your product can the model finish — and which step does the user need to feel they did?
toggles.note: Automation-vs-trust: on-device agents shift the unit of value from "a useful answer" to "a completed task", which changes what users want to see.

signals.title: Headline inflation reaccelerating — energy doing the lifting
signals.summary: Consumer prices heated back up, with energy responsible for most of the monthly jump. Services have stayed sticky underneath.

term_glossary.gloss: the broad measure of consumer prices
inflation excluding food and energy

percentile.label: Higher than 22% of observations in the last 10 years

chain.label: Signal
chain.text: CPI — the broad measure of consumer prices — turned higher again after a brief lull, with the latest reading meaningfully hotter than the months before it. Energy was the dominant driver.
chain.expansion: Headline CPI is sitting well above the Fed's 2% target. The bulk of the recent monthly increase traced back to energy categories; core services have stayed sticky underneath.

chain.label: Meaning
chain.text: The cooling narrative from earlier this year has reversed. A shock concentrated in one category (energy) is pulling the headline number up while services pressure has not gone away.
chain.expansion: When one volatile category drives the print, the temptation is to look through it — but consumers don't look through it. They feel it at the pump, on the utility bill, and in shipping costs.

chain.label: Product impact
chain.text: Customers are absorbing a fresh round of price pressure on the things they can't avoid. Discretionary spending is the first thing that gets squeezed when energy and rent eat more of the paycheck.
chain.expansion: If your product competes for non-essential spend, this is the kind of period where conversion slows and downgrade requests pick up before churn shows in the dashboard.

chain.label: Example
chain.text: Streaming and subscription services seeing softer upgrade rates when fuel and utility bills jump. Consumer-software trials taking longer to convert when households re-budget around essentials.
chain.expansion: Watch for revenue mix to shift toward the cheaper tier rather than churn outright.

chain.label: PM question
chain.text: If everyday prices are heating up again rather than cooling, does your pricing plan still assume an easier consumer than the one you actually have?
chain.expansion: Plans built on "inflation is fading" deserve a second look. The headline is not cooperating right now.

why_we_think_this.reasoning: After several months of cooler prints, headline CPI has stepped up two months in a row, with energy contributing the bulk of the latest monthly increase. Services have stayed sticky underneath rather than disinflating to meet the goods side.
counterarguments: Energy is volatile; a single quieter month could pull the headline back down.
Underlying services pressure could fade if wage growth slows.
why_we_think_this.what_would_make_us_wrong: Two consecutive monthly CPI prints back below the 3.0% YoY line would meaningfully weaken this read.

signals.reference_point: vs Fed 2% target · well above · reaccelerating

refined_why.evidence: Headline inflation stepped up again rather than continuing to cool, and energy did most of the work in the latest monthly increase. Services have stayed sticky underneath.
refined_why.counter_signal: Two consecutive monthly prints back below 3% would weaken this read.
refined_why.product_takeaway: Plans that quietly assumed inflation kept fading should be revisited — the current read says households are absorbing fresh pressure on essentials.

signals.title: Producer prices reaccelerating sharply — pipeline pressure is back
signals.summary: What businesses pay before passing costs through has jumped to the fastest pace in years. That kind of move shows up in consumer prices a few months later.

term_glossary.gloss: what producers pay before passing costs on to consumers

percentile.label: Higher than 18% of observations in the last 10 years

chain.label: Signal
chain.text: PPI — what producers pay before passing costs on to consumers — has jumped sharply, marking the fastest year-over-year reading in several years. Monthly pressure was broad: services and goods both pushed higher.
chain.expansion: PPI tends to lead CPI by 2–4 months for goods categories. A move of this size on the producer side rarely stays bottled up at the wholesale level.

chain.label: Meaning
chain.text: Input-cost pressure is back, not fading. The cost-push leg of inflation that looked like it had quieted earlier this year has reasserted itself.
chain.expansion: Energy-linked categories appear to be carrying a meaningful share, but the breadth across services and goods means it isn't purely a single-category story.

chain.label: Product impact
chain.text: Hardware, consumer-goods, and physical-product businesses are absorbing fresh margin pressure. The cleaner pricing window from earlier in the year is closing.
chain.expansion: Software businesses feel this indirectly: procurement budgets get tighter, deal cycles stretch, and customers push back on renewal price increases when their own input costs are rising.

chain.label: Example
chain.text: Consumer hardware brands quietly raising sticker prices after a quarter of holding the line. B2B SaaS deals slipping a quarter as buyers re-examine every recurring line item.
chain.expansion: Watch margin guidance turn cautious without volume changes — a classic pass-through tell.

chain.label: PM question
chain.text: Is there a cost line creeping back up while your pricing model still assumes it stays flat?
chain.expansion: If COGS is moving against you, the conversation shifts from "bank it" to "how do we hold price without bleeding customers."

why_we_think_this.reasoning: Producer-side cost pressure has stepped up sharply over the last two months after a quieter stretch, with strength across both goods and services components. Energy-linked categories appear to be doing meaningful work in the move.
counterarguments: Energy-driven spikes can fade in a single quieter month.
Some of the move may reflect tariff timing rather than underlying demand.
why_we_think_this.what_would_make_us_wrong: Two consecutive months of producer prices stepping back down to the 3% range would soften this read.

signals.reference_point: fastest pace in years · pipeline pressure back

refined_why.evidence: What businesses pay their suppliers has jumped sharply over the last couple of months after a quieter stretch. Energy-linked categories appear to be doing a lot of the work, but the breadth across services and goods is notable.
refined_why.counter_signal: Two months of producer prices stepping back down toward 3% YoY would soften this read.
refined_why.product_takeaway: Margin pressure is back on the table. If pricing was on autopilot during the calmer months, this is the moment to re-open the conversation.

signals.title: PCE running just above target — Fed's preferred gauge
signals.summary: The inflation measure the Fed actually watches has stalled — close to its target but not yet at it.

term_glossary.gloss: the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — broader than CPI

percentile.label: Higher than 26% of observations in the last 10 years

chain.label: Signal
chain.text: Core PCE — what the Fed actually targets — continues to run above its 2% goal. With CPI and PPI both reasserting upward pressure recently, the burden is on the Fed's preferred gauge to confirm whether disinflation is still on track.
chain.expansion: PCE differs from CPI in basket weights and substitution assumptions. The Fed treats it as the more reliable read.

chain.label: Meaning
chain.text: Inflation isn't where the Fed wants it. The neighbouring signals (CPI heating up, PPI reaccelerating) make it harder to call this benign.
chain.expansion: A flat reading near target is what policy-watchers describe as "stuck above 2." The risk is the read drifts higher rather than lower from here.

chain.label: Product impact
chain.text: Rate-cut timing remains uncertain. Companies planning big upfront spending on "cuts coming soon" may be planning on something that doesn't arrive.
chain.expansion: Even a single sticky data point can delay a cut cycle by a meeting.

chain.label: Example
chain.text: Mortgage-sensitive product categories, such as real-estate tech and consumer-lending apps, may face a longer cold spell than their roadmap assumes.
chain.expansion: Plan two scenarios: cuts arriving and cuts staying parked.

chain.label: PM question
chain.text: Does any part of your plan assume borrowing gets cheaper within six months?
chain.expansion: If yes, mark it as a dependency. The data does not currently support that assumption.

why_we_think_this.reasoning: Core PCE has remained in a narrow band above target for an extended period.
counterarguments: A growth slowdown could pull PCE lower quickly.
Energy shocks could push it higher.
why_we_think_this.what_would_make_us_wrong: Two consecutive PCE prints at or below 2.2% would change this read.

signals.reference_point: vs Fed 2% target · +0.6pp · stuck above target

refined_why.evidence: The inflation gauge the Fed actually steers by has been running above its 2% target. With CPI and PPI reasserting recently, the burden is on PCE to confirm whether disinflation is still on track.
refined_why.counter_signal: A sustained move clearly below the recent range would change this read.
refined_why.product_takeaway: Plans that assume rate cuts within six months should be flagged — the data doesn't support it yet.

signals.title: Money in the system has nudged back up — still below pre-tightening peaks
signals.summary: After a long stretch of slow drainage, the cash sloshing through the banking system has crept higher again over recent months without returning to old highs.

term_glossary.gloss: the money in the banking system available to lend
the Fed's total balance sheet — a proxy for liquidity provided

percentile.label: Higher than 50% of observations in the last 10 years

chain.label: Signal
chain.text: The Fed's balance sheet — a plain-English proxy for money moving through the system — drained for many months, then leveled off and has nudged modestly higher over the last several readings.
chain.expansion: The recent tick up is gentle, not a pivot. Levels still sit well below the post-2020 peaks but no longer below where they were a year ago.

chain.label: Meaning
chain.text: The squeeze has paused for now, but the system isn't flooded either. Conditions are neutral rather than aggressively easing or aggressively tightening.
chain.expansion: Where money is plentiful, risk gets funded. Where it's contracting, the cost of being wrong rises. Right now the picture is in between — useful to plan against, not to lean on.

chain.label: Product impact
chain.text: The capital backdrop is less hostile than it was twelve months ago, but it isn't the easy-money environment of 2020–2021. Long-horizon bets still carry a higher cost of patience than they used to.
chain.expansion: Plans that quietly assume conditions ease materially from here should be marked as a dependency rather than a base case.

chain.label: Example
chain.text: Late-stage growth companies finding raises possible but tougher than 2021 — capital is around, terms are more investor-friendly than they were.
chain.expansion: Watch for term-sheet structures that have become quietly more protective.

chain.label: PM question
chain.text: If liquidity stays in this neutral zone rather than easing further, what part of your roadmap quietly weakens?
chain.expansion: Identify the projects whose ROI assumes abundant capital. Flag them now, not later.

why_we_think_this.reasoning: WALCL drained steadily through the tightening cycle, but the latest several weekly readings have crept higher rather than continuing down. Reverse-repo balances are largely normalized; the recent uptick looks gradual rather than a regime change.
counterarguments: Short-term mechanical factors (TGA, repo) can move WALCL without changing the underlying stance.
A return to outright balance-sheet expansion would be a different story than a gentle nudge up.
why_we_think_this.what_would_make_us_wrong: Either a sustained resumption of monthly drawdowns or an explicit Fed pivot back to expanding the balance sheet would change this read.

signals.reference_point: below post-2020 peaks · gently higher in recent weeks

refined_why.evidence: The Fed balance sheet drained for many months, then leveled off and has nudged modestly higher in the latest weekly readings. Still well below post-2020 peaks.
refined_why.counter_signal: A sustained resumption of monthly drawdowns — or an explicit Fed pivot to outright expansion — would change this read.
refined_why.product_takeaway: The capital backdrop is neutral rather than easing. Plans that lean on liquidity loosening from here should be flagged as a dependency, not assumed.

signals.title: Long rates rangebound at elevated levels
signals.summary: The cost of long-term capital has stopped moving — for now.

term_glossary.gloss: the market's price for lending the US government money for 10 years — a benchmark for long-term capital costs

percentile.label: Higher than 5% of observations in the last 10 years

chain.label: Signal
chain.text: 10-year Treasury yields have traded in a broad band over recent months, with occasional sharp moves on individual auctions or data prints. They are not cheap, and they are not breaking lower.
chain.expansion: Rate volatility has flared on specific dates without breaking the band — inflation prints and fiscal-supply concerns have pulled yields up on intraday moves before easing back.

chain.label: Meaning
chain.text: Long-term borrowing costs have stabilized at levels that would have felt expensive five years ago.
chain.expansion: Stable-ish, not cheap. Discounted cash flow math is structurally different from pre-2022.

chain.label: Product impact
chain.text: Projects justified by "rates will fall" remain exposed. Projects that pay back quickly are safer.
chain.expansion: Long-duration features (infrastructure builds, broad platform plays) carry a higher cost of patience than they did.

chain.label: Example
chain.text: A two-year platform investment now competes against a low-risk government bond paying a real yield with zero execution risk.
chain.expansion: That comparison rarely shows up in roadmap reviews. It probably should.

chain.label: PM question
chain.text: Which part of your roadmap quietly assumes money will become cheap again?
chain.expansion: If the answer is most of it, the plan may be calibrated to a world that no longer exists.

why_we_think_this.reasoning: Yield range has compressed alongside falling rate-volatility measures.
counterarguments: A risk-off shock could re-widen the range quickly.
Fiscal supply could push yields higher.
why_we_think_this.what_would_make_us_wrong: A break below 4% or above 4.6% sustained for a month would change this read.

signals.reference_point: vs pre-2020 · elevated · range with occasional spikes

refined_why.evidence: The benchmark long-term interest rate has held in a broad range over recent months — not cheap, and occasionally testing the top of the range on individual data prints.
refined_why.counter_signal: A sustained move clearly below the recent range — or clearly above it — for a month would change this read.
refined_why.product_takeaway: A long-horizon bet now competes with a meaningful risk-free return. That comparison rarely makes it into roadmap reviews — but it should.

status_meta.reason: Data older than cadence stale threshold

signals.title: Series A deal volume materially below last year — capital concentrating
signals.summary: Fewer companies are getting funded than a year ago, but average round sizes have held up. The pool isn't shrinking — it's pooling into fewer winners, with AI absorbing a disproportionate share.

term_glossary.gloss: a startup's first institutional fundraising round — typically after early traction

chain.label: Signal
chain.text: Series A deal volume is running materially below last year by curated tracking, while average round size has held up. The capital pool isn't shrinking — it's pooling.
chain.expansion: AI-aligned companies are absorbing a disproportionate share of the dollars that are getting deployed.

chain.label: Meaning
chain.text: Fundraising has become a more selective filter than it was 24 months ago.
chain.expansion: The bar for the next round looks higher in time-in-market, in efficiency, and in retention.

chain.label: Product impact
chain.text: Investors may care more about whether customers stay and whether each dollar spent turns into durable growth.
chain.expansion: Signals like product-led growth, how much existing customers grow over time, margin, and payback carry more weight than growth-at-all-costs metrics did.

chain.label: Example
chain.text: Founders are raising smaller bridge rounds instead of full Series A rounds to make their cash last longer.
chain.expansion: Bridge rounds at flat valuations have become more common than they were.

chain.label: PM question
chain.text: If you had to raise on your last 90 days of usage data, what would the deck say?
chain.expansion: Try writing the slide. Notice which metrics survive the exercise — and which don't.

why_we_think_this.reasoning: Public funding data has shown declining round counts for several quarters; average round size has risen, consistent with concentration rather than total contraction.
counterarguments: A rate-cut cycle could reopen capital broadly.
AI-adjacent dollars could spill into other sectors.
why_we_think_this.what_would_make_us_wrong: Three consecutive months of broad-based Series A growth outside AI would change this read.

signals.reference_point: deal volume well below last year · AI absorbing the share

refined_why.evidence: Series A deal volume by curated tracking is materially below last year. Average size has held up — capital is concentrating into fewer companies, with AI absorbing a disproportionate share.
refined_why.counter_signal: Three months of broader Series A growth outside AI would change this read.
refined_why.product_takeaway: If you had to raise on your last 90 days of usage, ask which metrics still hold up — and which ones quietly don't.

signals.pill_label_short: Startup funding still concentrating into AI

signals.title: Model release pace accelerating again
signals.summary: Three frontier model updates in the last two weeks — capability frontier moving fast.

term_glossary.gloss: the leading-edge AI models that define what's currently possible

chain.label: Signal
chain.text: Several leading AI labs shipped meaningful model updates in the same two-week window.
chain.expansion: Updates spanned reasoning, multimodal, and on-device capability — not a single direction of improvement.

chain.label: Meaning
chain.text: AI capability is improving faster than most product roadmaps can react to.
chain.expansion: A capability that was experimental six months ago may now be table-stakes.

chain.label: Product impact
chain.text: Features that depended on "AI cannot do that yet" need re-checking quarterly, not annually.
chain.expansion: Moats built on current capability gaps tend to erode faster than moats built on distribution or data.

chain.label: Example
chain.text: On-device reasoning models that didn't exist a year ago are now shipping in mobile OS updates.
chain.expansion: When a capability moves from cloud-only to on-device, the cost curve breaks.

chain.label: PM question
chain.text: What assumption from six months ago about what AI cannot do no longer holds?
chain.expansion: Pick one. Audit the roadmap items that depend on it.

why_we_think_this.reasoning: Multiple independent labs released meaningful updates in close succession — a pattern consistent with sustained acceleration.
counterarguments: Release cadence is bursty by nature.
Headline updates may overstate capability change.
why_we_think_this.what_would_make_us_wrong: A two-month gap with no frontier-grade releases would weaken this read.

refined_why.evidence: Multiple labs shipped meaningful model updates in close succession, across reasoning, multimodal, and on-device.
refined_why.counter_signal: A two-month gap with no major releases would weaken this read.
refined_why.product_takeaway: Moats built on today’s capability gap erode faster than moats built on distribution or data.

signals.title: AI model costs keep falling sharply
signals.summary: Public list prices for comparable AI capability have continued to drop fast across major labs. The math on shipping AI features has moved meaningfully in the last few months.

term_glossary.gloss: the cost of running an AI model to answer one request
the listed price companies pay when their product calls an AI model

signals.current_unit: over the last three months for top AI model prices

chain.label: Signal
chain.text: Public list prices for comparable AI capability have continued to drop sharply across several major labs over the last few months — through both direct price cuts and the arrival of cheaper model tiers.
chain.expansion: Headline drops are tracked from list-price reductions and new model tiers — not from negotiated discounts. The pattern is consistent across labs, not a single outlier.

chain.label: Meaning
chain.text: Each AI call now costs meaningfully less than it did at the start of the year. Features that were "too expensive to ship" a year ago deserve a fresh look.
chain.expansion: Throughput-per-dollar has often improved even faster than headline price, because newer models are also faster.

chain.label: Product impact
chain.text: The case for building sooner has improved, but the advantage from "we figured out the cost" may not last long.
chain.expansion: If a competitor ships next quarter, they pay your current price. Cost advantage from one quarter ago is largely gone.

chain.label: Example
chain.text: AI features that broke even only at premium tiers a year ago now fit comfortably inside a lower paid tier — and in some cases inside a free tier — on similar usage.
chain.expansion: That changes the unit economics of inclusion into a free tier vs. paid plan.

chain.label: PM question
chain.text: Which AI feature would you ship today if it cost a fraction of what your last estimate assumed?
chain.expansion: Write the list. Some of those features are now feasible.

why_we_think_this.reasoning: Public price reductions occurred in similar windows across labs, consistent with competitive cost-curve compression.
counterarguments: Compute supply shocks could reverse the curve.
Quality-adjusted price may move slower than headline price.
why_we_think_this.what_would_make_us_wrong: A frontier-tier price increase from a major lab in the next two months would weaken this read.

refined_why.evidence: Public price cuts and cheaper model tiers from several major labs in roughly the same window. The direction and pace are clear even where specific percentage claims are approximate.
refined_why.counter_signal: A frontier-tier price increase from any major lab in the next two months would weaken this read.
refined_why.product_takeaway: Write the list of AI features you would ship at a fraction of last year's cost. Some of those just became feasible.

signals.title: Open-source AI gravity strengthening
signals.summary: Developer attention keeps concentrating on open-source tools for building AI agents.

term_glossary.gloss: AI models and frameworks released with publicly viewable weights or code

chain.label: Signal
chain.text: Open-source tools for building and coordinating AI agents are attracting more developers than a year ago.
chain.expansion: Activity concentrates in agents, evaluation tools, and AI running directly on devices rather than base-model training.

chain.label: Meaning
chain.text: Developer attention may be shifting toward the tools that connect AI systems together, not just the base models.
chain.expansion: Where attention pools, ecosystems form — and switching costs eventually accumulate there.

chain.label: Product impact
chain.text: Building on open-source agent tools may carry less ecosystem risk than it did twelve months ago.
chain.expansion: Dependencies stabilize as communities form. They're less stable when they're early-experimental.

chain.label: Example
chain.text: Several agent tools that did not exist eighteen months ago are now appearing in enterprise architecture guides.
chain.expansion: Watch what reference architectures from large customers actually name.

chain.label: PM question
chain.text: Is there a piece of your stack better served by an open-source layer than a closed vendor today?
chain.expansion: Audit one component. The answer may have flipped.

why_we_think_this.reasoning: Sustained increases in stars and contributors on agent-related repos over 12+ months.
counterarguments: Stars are vanity-prone metrics.
Ecosystem activity can move quickly to new repos.
why_we_think_this.what_would_make_us_wrong: A sustained slowdown in contributor counts across the top frameworks would weaken this read.

refined_why.evidence: Open-weight models are catching up on the benchmarks people actually use, and adoption is moving from researchers into product teams.
refined_why.counter_signal: A multi-quarter pause in open-weight releases would weaken this read.
refined_why.product_takeaway: Anywhere you’ve standardized on one closed model, the lock-in is weaker than it was a year ago.

signals.title: Compute cost curve still bending downward
signals.summary: Cloud provider costs keep improving. The change is slower than AI model pricing, but still consistent.

term_glossary.gloss: the underlying processing power needed to run AI workloads
large cloud providers — AWS, Azure, Google Cloud — that supply most AI compute

chain.label: Signal
chain.text: The cost of running AI workloads in the cloud continues to decline.
chain.expansion: Improvements stem from chip generations, software efficiency, and contract-pricing competition.

chain.label: Meaning
chain.text: Running the work is getting cheaper, even where the sticker price of high-end chips has not fallen.
chain.expansion: Cost per useful work matters more for product economics than chip price.

chain.label: Product impact
chain.text: Workloads that were marginal a year ago may be profitable now.
chain.expansion: Background AI features (summaries, suggestions, drafts) become cheaper to keep on by default.

chain.label: Example
chain.text: Always-on AI assistants in productivity tools are increasingly economical even on free tiers.
chain.expansion: That re-opens the question of what to give away vs. what to gate.

chain.label: PM question
chain.text: Which AI capability would you turn on for everyone if the cost of each extra use were cut in half?
chain.expansion: Some of those capabilities may now be in range.

why_we_think_this.reasoning: Multiple hyperscalers commented on improving per-workload economics over consecutive quarters.
counterarguments: Aggregate cost reductions can mask category-specific spikes.
Hyperscaler commentary is incentive-aligned to look favorable.
why_we_think_this.what_would_make_us_wrong: A reversal in per-workload commentary at one or more major hyperscaler would soften this read.

signals.reference_point: vs 12mo ago · -14% · cheaper at the workload level

refined_why.evidence: Cost per unit of useful AI work keeps dropping — across hardware, model efficiency, and serving stacks.
refined_why.counter_signal: A sustained supply shock in AI hardware would change this read.
refined_why.product_takeaway: Features that were too expensive to ship last year deserve a fresh look — the math has moved.

signals.title: Retail sales steady — consumer still showing up
signals.summary: Spending hasn't broken. It also hasn't accelerated.

term_glossary.gloss: the dollar value of goods sold by retailers — a near-real-time read on consumer demand

percentile.label: Higher than 37% of observations in the last 10 years

chain.label: Signal
chain.text: Retail sales are running roughly in line with the last six months — steady, neither accelerating nor breaking.
chain.expansion: Discretionary categories (restaurants, electronics) sit slightly below the headline; essentials slightly above.

chain.label: Meaning
chain.text: Consumer demand is holding without showing momentum in either direction.
chain.expansion: Not a story of strength or weakness — a story of equilibrium.

chain.label: Product impact
chain.text: Demand planning may safely assume the category stays steady. Growth will likely need to come from winning share, not from the whole market rising.
chain.expansion: When the category isn't growing, your growth comes from someone else's customers.

chain.label: Example
chain.text: Subscription-commerce brands shifting marketing from finding new customers to getting more value from existing customers.
chain.expansion: When acquisition is harder, monetization gets a roadmap slot it didn't have last year.

chain.label: PM question
chain.text: If category demand stays flat, which lever do you actually have to grow?
chain.expansion: Audit roadmap items that secretly assume macro tailwinds.

why_we_think_this.reasoning: Headline retail sales have stayed in a tight range; survey data hasn't broken either direction.
counterarguments: Labor softening could pull retail down quickly.
A rate-cut cycle could lift it just as quickly.
why_we_think_this.what_would_make_us_wrong: A drop below 1% YoY for two consecutive months would change this read.

refined_why.evidence: Consumer spending is steady — not soaring, not falling. Surveys back this up.
refined_why.counter_signal: A year-over-year drop below 1% for two months running would change this read.
refined_why.product_takeaway: When category demand is flat, growth comes from taking share. Audit anything in your roadmap that assumes a rising tide.

signals.title: Consumer confidence near record lows — inflation expectations elevated
signals.summary: How households feel about the economy has crumbled to readings rarely seen. Year-ahead inflation expectations are uncomfortably high underneath.

term_glossary.gloss: a survey-based measure of how households feel about their financial future

signals.source_note: University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment · via FRED

percentile.label: Lower than 99% of observations in the last 10 years

chain.label: Signal
chain.text: The University of Michigan consumer sentiment index is sitting near readings only seen during major shocks — not drifting lower, sunk to the floor. Year-ahead inflation expectations from the same survey are running uncomfortably high.
chain.expansion: Households are simultaneously telling surveyors they feel bad about the economy and that they expect prices to keep rising at a meaningful pace over the next year. That combination usually shows up in how people spend.

chain.label: Meaning
chain.text: This isn't cautious-not-alarmed anymore. Sentiment is at the kind of level that historically lines up with households tightening, trading down, and stalling discretionary purchases.
chain.expansion: Hard data (jobs, retail) hasn't broken to match yet — but soft data this weak rarely co-exists with hard data this steady for long.

chain.label: Product impact
chain.text: Discretionary purchases, premium tiers, and bigger-ticket consumer spend are where this shows up first. Free tiers and obvious entry points become more important than they were three months ago.
chain.expansion: When households expect prices to keep rising, the willingness to lock in a new monthly bill drops noticeably.

chain.label: Example
chain.text: Premium subscription downgrades picking up before churn shows. Bigger-ticket consumer software trials taking longer to convert, with more requests for cheaper plans.
chain.expansion: Sales and onboarding flows that depend on quick conversion may need more patience — and a cheaper landing tier — built in.

chain.label: PM question
chain.text: If your customer feels noticeably worse about the economy than they did six months ago, does your pricing page still make the cheapest path obvious?
chain.expansion: Audit the entry tier and the downgrade path. Both matter more when sentiment is this low.

why_we_think_this.reasoning: The Michigan headline is sitting at levels historically associated with major shocks, and inflation expectations within the same survey are elevated. Survey weakness has been broad rather than concentrated in one demographic slice.
counterarguments: Sentiment surveys have grown more politically polarized post-2020 — the level may overstate how much real behavior has shifted.
Hard spending data has not yet broken to match the soft data.
why_we_think_this.what_would_make_us_wrong: A sustained recovery in the headline sentiment index combined with inflation expectations easing back toward 3% would weaken this read.

sources.name: University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment (via FRED)

signals.reference_point: near record lows on the Michigan series

refined_why.evidence: The Michigan sentiment headline is sitting at levels rarely seen, and year-ahead inflation expectations are elevated. Households are telling surveyors they feel bad and expect prices to keep rising.
refined_why.counter_signal: A sustained recovery in headline sentiment combined with inflation expectations easing back toward 3% would change this read.
refined_why.product_takeaway: When households feel this stressed and expect prices to keep rising, the cheaper path through your product matters more than the premium one.

signals.title: Personal agents and on-device AI utilities climbing
signals.summary: Consumer attention rotating toward AI utilities that live on the phone, not the cloud.

term_glossary.gloss: an AI app that takes actions on behalf of a single user rather than just answering questions
AI features that run locally on the phone or laptop without sending data to a server

signals.source_note: Triangulated: app charts + Product Hunt + GitHub trending

percentile.label: Highest pattern density we've tracked since 2021

chain.label: Signal
chain.text: Personal agents and on-device AI utilities are showing up in app charts, GitHub trending, and Product Hunt simultaneously — a pattern that wasn't there six months ago.
chain.expansion: Triangulated across surfaces, not a single chart. We're describing momentum, not rankings.

chain.label: Meaning
chain.text: Consumer attention may be rotating toward AI products that do something specific for one person, rather than chat about everything.
chain.expansion: The shift from "AI as conversation" to "AI as agent" looks like it's leaking into mainstream consumer software.

chain.label: Product impact
chain.text: Products built around "ask a model" workflows may need to evolve toward "the model already did it."
chain.expansion: The unit of value may shift from a useful answer to a completed task.

chain.label: Example
chain.text: Note apps that summarize and act on calendar items without being asked. Mobile utilities that quietly clean photos overnight.
chain.expansion: When automation happens behind the user, the surface area for branding and pricing changes.

chain.label: PM question
chain.text: What workflow still assumes more people instead of better tools?
chain.expansion: If your product still hands work to the user, ask whether the model could quietly finish it.

why_we_think_this.reasoning: The same kinds of apps keep surfacing across independent charts. We are describing the pattern, not the rank of any single app.
counterarguments: Chart movements can be marketing-driven.
Triangulation can produce false coherence.
why_we_think_this.what_would_make_us_wrong: If these categories quietly disappear from top charts in the next quarter, the pattern weakens.

refined_why.evidence: Personal-agent and on-device AI utilities are showing up on app charts, GitHub, and Product Hunt in the same window.
refined_why.counter_signal: If these categories quietly fall off the top charts next quarter, the pattern weakens.
refined_why.product_takeaway: If your product still hands work to the user, ask whether the model could quietly finish it.

signals.title: Payrolls slowing — direction, not crisis
signals.summary: Hiring is cooler than a year ago. It hasn't broken.

term_glossary.gloss: the monthly count of jobs added across most of the US economy — the headline labor read

percentile.label: Lower than 71% of observations in the last 10 years

chain.label: Signal
chain.text: Monthly payroll prints have been choppy — strong months followed by weak ones — but the trend line is clearly cooler than 2022–2023. The labor market is slowing without falling apart.
chain.expansion: Strength remains in healthcare and government. Tech, finance, and discretionary services have softened more.

chain.label: Meaning
chain.text: The labor market is cooling without breaking.
chain.expansion: Cooling, not contracting — but the direction is unambiguous.

chain.label: Product impact
chain.text: Employers have a little more leverage in hiring than they did a year ago.
chain.expansion: Wage-cost pressure should ease at the margin; backfill speed should improve.

chain.label: Example
chain.text: Engineering teams seeing fewer competing offers per finalist than in 2024.
chain.expansion: That changes negotiation dynamics for senior hires more than entry-level ones.

chain.label: PM question
chain.text: What plan is implicitly built on a labor market that no longer exists?
chain.expansion: Audit one workforce assumption. The market it was built for may have rolled forward.

why_we_think_this.reasoning: Payrolls, openings, and quit rates have all softened in similar windows.
counterarguments: Revisions can shift the picture meaningfully.
Sector mix can mislead.
why_we_think_this.what_would_make_us_wrong: Two consecutive prints above 200k would weaken this read.

signals.reference_point: trend cooler than 2022–2023 · still net positive

refined_why.evidence: Monthly hiring is slower than 2022–2023, but still positive and broad-based.
refined_why.counter_signal: Three months of net job losses would change this read.
refined_why.product_takeaway: Cooler hiring is the soft kind, not the crisis kind. Budgeting can move; panic shouldn’t.

signals.title: Tech hiring remains near multi-year lows — softness broad
signals.summary: Layoffs continue. Hiring stays soft. The pattern is wider than the biggest tech companies, not just headline-name cuts.

term_glossary.gloss: the pace at which technology companies are adding people — relative to recent history

chain.label: Signal
chain.text: Tech-sector hiring remains near multi-year lows by our composite tracking. Layoff activity has stayed elevated. The softness has widened beyond the largest companies.
chain.expansion: Reading layoffs.fyi alone would overstate the call — triangulating with BLS payroll detail and earnings commentary supports a wider read.

chain.label: Meaning
chain.text: Engineering hiring is tight even though specific roles (ML, infra) still see competition.
chain.expansion: The barbell is real: scarce skills competed for, broader roles softening.

chain.label: Product impact
chain.text: Teams may choose partners, vendors, or AI tools when they cannot add enough people internally.
chain.expansion: Internal headcount becomes harder to add. The cost of saying yes to a project is now mostly the cost of saying no to another.

chain.label: Example
chain.text: Teams adopting AI coding tools or design tools to keep moving without adding more people.
chain.expansion: Watch for tool adoption that closes capacity gaps rather than enables new ambition.

chain.label: PM question
chain.text: If you can't hire two more engineers, which roadmap item gets postponed — and which gets quietly handed to AI tooling?
chain.expansion: Force-rank the roadmap against current capacity. Make the trade-off explicit.

why_we_think_this.reasoning: Multiple sources align: layoffs trend, payroll subsector data, and earnings commentary all point in the same direction.
counterarguments: Sector-specific dynamics could be confused for a broader pattern.
Layoff data over-indexes on visible cuts.
why_we_think_this.what_would_make_us_wrong: Two consecutive months of net hiring growth across major tech subsectors would change this read.

signals.reference_point: near multi-year lows on the composite

refined_why.evidence: Tech-sector hiring sits near multi-year lows by our composite tracking — across layoff trackers, government subsector data, and earnings commentary. Softness is broader than just headline-name cuts.
refined_why.counter_signal: Two months of net hiring growth across major tech subsectors would change this read.
refined_why.product_takeaway: If two more engineers aren't coming, which roadmap item gets postponed — and which quietly gets handed to AI tooling?

signals.title: AI rulemaking accelerating at the state level
signals.summary: Federal AI rules are slow. State and EU rules aren't waiting.

term_glossary.gloss: the EU's framework regulating AI by risk category — being phased in through 2026

signals.source_note: EU AI Act tracker + state legislatures · curated

chain.label: Signal
chain.text: State-level AI bills and EU AI Act phase-ins are arriving at a faster cadence than a year ago.
chain.expansion: Topics cluster around transparency, deepfakes, automated decisioning, and youth safety.

chain.label: Meaning
chain.text: Compliance planning is shifting from "wait for one federal answer" to "handle state-by-state and EU rules now."
chain.expansion: Patchwork compliance can become a meaningful product-roadmap cost long before federal harmonization arrives.

chain.label: Product impact
chain.text: Features that touch automated decisions, identity, or minors may need different versions in different regions.
chain.expansion: Data flows and disclosures may need re-wiring before launch in specific jurisdictions.

chain.label: Example
chain.text: Consumer apps adding deepfake-disclosure flows in EU launches before US ones.
chain.expansion: Watch where flows diverge by region — that's a regulation tell.

chain.label: PM question
chain.text: Which features assume a single global UX that may not survive 2026?
chain.expansion: Identify the geo-fragile pieces of the roadmap and brief legal early.

why_we_think_this.reasoning: Multiple jurisdictions are advancing AI rules independently. The cumulative pace matters more than any single action.
counterarguments: State bills frequently die in committee.
Enforcement timelines often slip.
why_we_think_this.what_would_make_us_wrong: A federal preemption package would consolidate the landscape rapidly.

refined_why.evidence: More U.S. states have moved on AI rules this year than in any prior year, mostly around disclosure, training data, and decision systems.
refined_why.counter_signal: A federal preemption framework would shift this from many small rule sets to one larger one.
refined_why.product_takeaway: Anywhere your product makes a decision about a person, write down today how you’d explain it tomorrow.

signals.title: Regional manufacturing activity slipped back negative
signals.summary: Philly Fed manufacturers were modestly downbeat last month — one regional read, not the national picture. ISM, the national index, is running more upbeat right now; the gap between them is the part worth watching.

term_glossary.gloss: the share of firms reporting growth minus the share reporting contraction — above zero means more firms are growing than shrinking
the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia's monthly survey of manufacturers in its district (eastern PA, southern NJ, Delaware) — a regional proxy for U.S. factory activity

signals.source_note: Philadelphia Fed Manufacturing Business Outlook Survey · via FRED

percentile.label: Lower than 73% of observations in the last 10 years

chain.label: Signal
chain.text: The Philadelphia Fed's monthly survey of manufacturers — a regional proxy for national factory activity — dropped from clearly expanding to barely-below-zero in a single month. New orders and shipments fell with it.
chain.expansion: The diffusion index moves in big monthly steps because it captures change-from-last-month, not levels. The honest read is direction-of-travel, not the absolute number.

chain.label: Meaning
chain.text: Factory orders aren't growing right now. Survey moves this sharp usually show up in hard manufacturing data — production, shipments, hiring — a few months later.
chain.expansion: Regional Fed surveys lead the national hard data by roughly two to three months. A single soft month is noise; a second one is a pattern.

chain.label: Product impact
chain.text: If you sell into manufacturers, procurement cycles tighten quickly when surveys turn. If your product depends on the goods economy moving (logistics, hardware, B2B physical-world tools), this is a leading tell.
chain.expansion: Software margins insulate you, but pipeline timelines from industrial buyers stretch when their own forward orders soften.

chain.label: Example
chain.text: B2B vendors selling to industrial customers reporting longer sales cycles when regional Fed surveys turn negative. Capital-equipment trials get parked behind cash-preservation discussions.
chain.expansion: Watch for renewal-rate drift before churn — industrial buyers downgrade tiers before they cancel.

chain.label: PM question
chain.text: If factory activity stays soft, which forecast in your plan secretly assumes industrial buyers keep spending the way they did a quarter ago?
chain.expansion: Worth flagging that assumption explicitly rather than letting it ride.

signals_used: Philadelphia Fed Manufacturing Business Outlook Survey (FRED GACDFSA066MSFRBPHI)
why_we_think_this.reasoning: We use the Philly Fed's monthly diffusion index as our manufacturing-activity proxy because it is the most established free regional Fed survey of factory conditions, is published with no paywall via FRED, and has historically tracked national manufacturing turns reasonably well. We do not publish the proprietary ISM Manufacturing PMI — that data is not freely auto-fetchable.
counterarguments: This is one Federal Reserve district, not the national economy — single-month moves can reflect local effects.
The diffusion index captures month-over-month change, not absolute levels, so it can whipsaw.
why_we_think_this.what_would_make_us_wrong: Two consecutive months back above +10 would weaken the soft-activity read.

sources.name: Philadelphia Fed Manufacturing Business Outlook Survey (via FRED GACDFSA066MSFRBPHI)

signals.reference_point: regional Fed proxy · not the proprietary national ISM PMI

refined_why.evidence: The Philly Fed's monthly read on factory activity flipped from clearly expanding to flat-to-negative in a single month. New orders and shipments fell with it.
refined_why.counter_signal: Two months back above +10 would weaken this read.
refined_why.product_takeaway: If you sell into manufacturers or the goods economy, pipeline forecasts that assume the last quarter's buying pace are worth re-examining.

signals.title: Regional services activity still in contraction
signals.summary: Dallas Fed services firms reported softening conditions — a Texas-skewed read, not national. Watch whether ISM Services, the national equivalent, confirms or diverges over the next release cycle.

term_glossary.gloss: growth or contraction at non-manufacturing firms — restaurants, software, professional services, transport, healthcare
the Dallas Fed's monthly survey of service-sector firms in Texas — a regional proxy for U.S. services activity, used here because no comparable national services index is freely auto-fetchable

signals.source_note: Dallas Fed Texas Service Sector Outlook Survey · via FRED

percentile.label: Lower than 66% of observations in the last 10 years

chain.label: Signal
chain.text: The Dallas Fed's monthly survey of service-sector firms — our regional proxy for national services activity — has been below zero for several consecutive months. The latest read got worse, not better.
chain.expansion: Services are roughly 70% of U.S. economic activity, so a multi-month soft patch in a representative regional survey is worth tracking even if it isn't the national ISM.

chain.label: Meaning
chain.text: Services firms are reporting more contraction than expansion month after month. That lines up with the soft consumer-sentiment read elsewhere in Pulse — soft data is broad-based right now, not isolated.
chain.expansion: A single negative diffusion month is normal noise. Several in a row, paired with weak sentiment, is a pattern that usually precedes slower services hiring.

chain.label: Product impact
chain.text: If you sell into services businesses — agencies, restaurants, professional firms, healthcare practices — budget conversations tighten quickly when survey data sits negative for months. Renewals get scrutinized; new tools get deferred.
chain.expansion: B2B SaaS pipelines into services verticals are the most exposed; consumer-facing software is exposed indirectly via softer hiring at those firms.

chain.label: Example
chain.text: Vertical SaaS tools for service businesses (salons, agencies, clinics, contractors) reporting longer evaluation cycles and more 'pause' decisions than usual.
chain.expansion: Watch for trial-to-paid conversion to slow before churn picks up — buyers stretch evaluations before they outright leave.

chain.label: PM question
chain.text: Where does your roadmap assume services-sector customers are still in growth mode? Pick the one most exposed and ask whether it deserves a downside scenario this quarter.
chain.expansion: The honest answer to 'are services-sector buyers spending like a year ago?' right now is: not really.

signals_used: Dallas Fed Texas Service Sector Outlook Survey (FRED TSSOSBACTUAMFRBDAL)
why_we_think_this.reasoning: We use the Dallas Fed's monthly services diffusion index as our services-activity proxy because it is the most established free regional Fed survey of services conditions, is published with no paywall via FRED, and covers a large, diversified state economy. We do not publish the proprietary ISM Services PMI — that data is not freely auto-fetchable.
counterarguments: This is one state, not the U.S. — Texas-specific factors (energy mix, immigration policy) can pull the index around.
Diffusion indexes capture month-over-month change, so they can lag turning points in absolute levels.
why_we_think_this.what_would_make_us_wrong: Two consecutive months back above zero would weaken the soft-services read.

sources.name: Dallas Fed Texas Service Sector Outlook Survey (via FRED TSSOSBACTUAMFRBDAL)

signals.reference_point: regional Fed proxy · not the proprietary national ISM Services PMI

refined_why.evidence: The Dallas Fed services survey has been negative for several months in a row, with the latest read worse than the one before it. Soft survey data is broad-based right now, not isolated.
refined_why.counter_signal: Two months back above zero would weaken this read.
refined_why.product_takeaway: If you sell into services businesses, plans that assume the last year's buying pace deserve a downside scenario this quarter.

source_philosophy.intro: Pulse reads from a three-tier source system. Tier 1 drives conclusions. Tier 2 supports and triangulates. Tier 3 informs framing but never drives a claim on its own.

tiers.label: Primary
tiers.examples: Fed, BLS, Treasury, BEA, FRED, Census — official datasets we cite directly.

tiers.label: Market & product
tiers.examples: GitHub, Hugging Face, Product Hunt, lab pricing pages, earnings calls, curated funding summaries.

tiers.label: Editorial & context
tiers.examples: Regulation trackers, podcasts, newsletters, X — used for framing, not as evidence.

phase_meta.data_layer: structured sample with stable Tier-1 sources scaffolded; curated/sample values for fragile Tier-2/3 signals.
